paragraphs.heading: The unit of life
paragraphs.text: A cell is the basic unit of structure and function in every living thing. The name comes from the Latin cellula, a small room. At its simplest, a cell is a membrane that lets some things through, wrapped around the cytoplasm, which holds the genetic material. Most cells can only be seen through a microscope. Apart from highly specialised kinds, such as red blood cells and gametes, most can copy themselves and make proteins.

paragraphs.heading: Two big groups
paragraphs.text: All living things are sorted into two groups. Prokaryotes, which include bacteria and archaea, are always single cells and have no nucleus wrapped in membrane; their DNA sits in a region called the nucleoid. Eukaryotes can be single cells or many-celled, and keep their nucleus inside a nuclear membrane. Animals, plants, most fungi and some algae are eukaryotes.

paragraphs.heading: Compartments inside
paragraphs.text: Eukaryotic cells also hold other compartments wrapped in membrane, called organelles. Mitochondria supply energy for the cell's work, and chloroplasts in plants make sugars through photosynthesis. Some organelles have no membrane at all, such as ribosomes, which both groups have in somewhat different forms. Prokaryotic cells are smaller and simpler, and lack a nucleus and the other membrane-bound organelles usually present in eukaryotes.

paragraphs.heading: A bacterium's coat
paragraphs.text: A bacterium is enclosed in a protective cell envelope. Usually this is a plasma membrane covered by a cell wall, and some bacteria add a gel-like capsule on top. The envelope gives the cell its stiffness and screens it from its surroundings. The wall, made of peptidoglycan, also keeps the cell from swelling and bursting from osmotic pressure when its surroundings are hypotonic. Inside, the DNA is usually a single circular chromosome lying in direct contact with the cytoplasm, in the nucleoid.

paragraphs.heading: From specks to centimetres
paragraphs.text: Most prokaryotes are the smallest organisms of all, between 0.1 and 5.0 μm across. Yet the largest known bacterium, Thiomargarita magnifica, can be seen with the naked eye. It averages 1 cm long and can reach 2 cm.

paragraphs.heading: How cells were found
paragraphs.text: Cells appeared on Earth around four billion years ago. Robert Hooke found them in 1665 and named them for their likeness to the cells of a monastery. In 1838 and 1839, Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann showed that plants and animals are built from cells as their basic structural unit. Their cell theory holds that every organism is made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and that each cell comes from an earlier cell.
